Author: Cypko, M.; Stoehr, M.; Amft, O.
Title: Enhancing clinical decision support with large language models: A semi-automatic approach for modeling Bayesian networks
Publication Title: International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery
Abstract Note: Purpose Bayesian networks (BNs) have proven to be a particularly transparent and comprehensible tool in clinical decision support systems, medical diagnostics, and treatment planning [1]. BNs can model complex probabilistic relationships between different clinical variables and combine empirical data with expert knowledge to facilitate informed decision making under uncertainty. The challenge in creating decision graphs for large-scale networks is that knowledge modeling from clinical guidelines is rarely automated so far and thus remains a very time-consuming, manual, expert-driven task. As shown in an example of laryngeal cancer [1], modeling of multi-disciplinary treatment decision can take several years to complete.The integration of large language models (LLMs), e.g., ChatGPT by Open AI, into the modeling process has the potential to reduce the amount of time and expertise required, but also opens up new ways to incorporate evolving medical knowledge and data-driven insights into the long-term maintenance of knowledge bases. Methods Our methodology combines experience in modeling clinical decision graphs with the advanced capabilities of LLMs. Our approach is twofold: Firstly, our approach applies a graph structure that distin-guishes between different variable types, enabling the modelling of comprehensive multidisciplinary therapy decisions [1]. In addition, it adheres to a structured modeling and validation workflow with domain experts [1].Second, our approach adheres to the prompt guidelines provided by OpenAI and the scientific ChatGPT community [2]. Relevant guideline recommendations for our approach are: (a) to provide a reference text to limit the scope of the LLM model and (b) to break down complex tasks into simpler subtasks using different strategies. Furthermore, (c) LLM models should be represented by ''chains of thought'', otherwise an LLM model can quickly provide inappropriate answers. In order to be able to better evaluate more extensive results, (d) the prompts to the LLM should be requested for output in JSON format. In addition, (e) external tools can be used for efficient and more precise knowledge retrieval, and (f) systematic testing is rec-ommended to ensure accuracy and reliability. ResultsWe present a conceptual approach for semi-automatically modeling of BNs graphs for clinical decision support using LLMs. The process is structured into six strategic steps (see also Fig. 1):In steps 1-2, the scope of the LLM model is reduced both syn-tactically and clinically through the use of reference texts. A reference text with syntactic guidelines for modeling BNs in a clinical context is created by a knowledge engineer and is independent of the clinical use case. The clinical reference texts include choosing appropriate clinical guidelines and studies. This task depends on the specific context of the modeling and is carried out by domain experts.In the following Steps 3 and 4a/b, a BN is semi-automatically constructed with references to the guidelines in JSON format. The modeling begins in Step 3 with the definition of the start variable and then proceeds to iterative and interconnected Steps 4a and 4b, in order to extend the graph by defining relevant ancestors and descendances of already modeled nodes. In the modelling steps, the LLM helps to suggest relevant variables, events, and references to the previously defined clinical guidelines and studies. While the other steps 1,2,5, and 6 only require instructions from the user (e.g. providing guide-lines), the modeling Steps 3 and 4a/b are intended as an active exchange between the expert who provides clinical knowledge and the LLM. The scope of support provided by the LLM (i.e. whether, how many and which types of clinical variables, events and references should be suggested by the LLM) depends on the knowledge of the domain expert and is adjusted in each interactive modeling step given the user prompts. For clinical evaluation, graph modelling should alsobe supported by a suitable graph visualization and the graph should be updated with each modelling step. While the modeling is basically carried out via prompts, the graphical representation ensures trans-parency and comprehensibility of the modeling process for the experts and enables them to evaluate the graph and adjust it if nec-essary. For syntactical correctness, automated tests with predefined prompts should also be carried out in the modeling steps to check whether the graph complies with the predefined syntax of the BN.In the last two steps 5 and 6, the syntax can be adjusted, and both the variables and event names in the network are rewritten using established nomenclatures (e.g., SNOMED CT), as well as converted into a more application-specific format, e.g., the HL7 standard format FHIR. ConclusionThis work demonstrates a novel integration of LLMs, in particular Chat GPT, into the semi-automatic construction of BNs for clinical decision support. By reducing the modeling effort, ensuring clinical correctness, and refining the network through expert evaluation, we achieve a scalable and adaptable approach. The LLM-BN model not only streamlines the development process, but also meets the high demands of a clinical environment. Future research shall focus on defining guidelines for selecting suitable reference texts and prompts, which are critical in the context of developing BNs for clinical decision support systems. We will then test our approach using val-idated models, e.g. using [1] and attempt to reconstruct the original BN. Finally, suitable modeling tools shall be created to better com-bine and automate the LLM-based modeling and validation workflow.

Author: Kim, D.-Y.; Jang, B.-S.; Kim, E.; Chie, E.K.
Title: Integrating deep learning-based dose distribution prediction with Bayesian networks for decision support in respiratory motion controlled radiotherapy
Abstract Note: Background: Selecting the better of the two institutionally available techniques to harbor optimal motion management, either a high dose rate stereotactic linear accelerator delivery using TrueBeam (TBX) or Magnetic Resonance (MR)-guided gated delivery using MRIdian (MRG), can be time-consuming and costly as independent treatment plan generation is a prerequisite. To address this challenge, we aimed to develop a decision-supporting algorithm that predicts the optimal treatment modality based on a combination of deep learning-generated dose distributions and relevant clinical data. Methods: Clinical data and images were collected for 65 patients diagnosed with primary liver cancer (N=40) and pancreatic cancer (N=25) to facilitate the development of a predictive model for RT dose distribution. Treatment plans were created for both TBX and MRG. A three-dimensional U-Net deep learning approach was employed to predict RT dose distribution and generate dose volume histograms (DVHs). Generated DVH profiles were included in the Bayesian network (BN) decision-supporting algorithm by incorporating clinical data to nominate superior treatment plan. Results: The root-mean-square error (RMSE) of voxels between the ground truth and the predictive dose from developed model was 3.04 (with a range of 2.29 to 3.79). The RMSE for the MRG prediction model was lower than that of the TBX. In general, the predictive normalized DVH metrics demonstrated superior performance in the MRG prediction models. Then, a BN model was established for determining the optimal treatment plan. The BN structure incorporated factors such as age, tumor volume, tumor to hollow viscus relationship as abutting vs apart, and the normalized value of the maximum dose to the neighboring dose limiting organ for MRG. The overall area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.84. Conclusions: We demonstrated a decision-supporting algorithm that could provide guidance to clinicians to select the superior plan from two competing RT systems for upper GI malignancy. This is anticipated to save resources in terms of manpower, time, and cost for both care-provider and the patient. Legal entity responsible for the study: The authors. Author: Bechny, M.; Fiorillo, L.; Scutari, M.; van der Meer, J.; Schmidt, M.; Bassetti, C.; Tzovara, A.; Faraci, F.
Title: Expert-informed Bayesian networks for sleep diagnosis support system: A proof-of-concept study
Abstract Note: Introduction: A clinical sleep-study is typically undertaken by individuals suspected of having a sleep-disorder. Therefore, collected data are non-randomized, with a high degree of confounding yielding distributional shifts, where disordered individuals are typically genderspecific and older. Using such data, it is challenging to create reliable AI-models assessing the risk of diseases based on observed variables (e.g., demographics, markers of sleep-architecture). Another challenge lies in the often simultaneous presence of multiple sleep-disorders. Method: AI black-box algorithms rarely provide reasoning behind their judgments, a strict requirement for healthcare. In contrast, Bayesian networks (BN), aiming to construct and quantify the cause-effect relationships between variables, represent a compromise between leveraging the potential of big-data to facilitate physicians' work and ensuring explainable predictions. The use of BN involves two steps: (i) structure-learning to identify dependencies between variables, and (ii) inference to quantify them. A priori knowledge on cause-effect relations can be encoded in BN, dramatically reducing computations. Once the structure and parameters of the BN are learnt, the resulting model can be used both for classification, to estimate the risk of one or more sleep-disorders, and for simulating interventions to explore how sleep-characteristics would change if a given subject were treated. Results: Our ongoing study utilizing the Berner-Sleep-Data-Base develops a BN that identifies relationships among demographic (e.g., age, gender), clinical (e.g., sleep diagnoses, AHI), and polysomnographic data (e.g., sleep-stage percentages, REM latency). By aggregating responses from questionnaires distributed to sleep specialists about cause-effect relationships between these variables, the knowledge consensus is used for constrained structure-learning. This approach increases the transparency and credibility of our model and simplifies computations by significantly reducing the search space. The resulting BN can serve as a screening tool in clinical settings and guide the development of novel digital biomarkers through simulations of hypothetical interventions: causal counterfactuals. Conclusion: Applying automated decision-support systems in clinical practice demands high transparency and explainability. Our study proposes a proof-of-concept solution based on BN, combining expertknowledge with rich clinical data. If successful, we plan to expand the BN to include additional variables (e.g., non-sleep comorbidities, medication, micro-events of sleep) and validate it on external databases.

Author: Zheng, S.; Xu, X.W.; Hu, Z.; Wang, M.; Yao, Y.; Li, J.
Title: Development and implementation of a guideline-based decision support system for etiological diagnosis of Sustained Monomorphic Ventricular Tachycardia (SMVT)
Abstract Note: Background: Guideline (GL)-based decision support systems (DSSs) play a significant role in supporting physicians in their decision-making processes by providing structured clinical guidance. While these systems have shown significant success in enhancing practitioner performance and patient outcomes in general practice, their application in the context of ventricular arrhythmias remains limited. Moreover, the clinical etiological diagnosis of ventricular arrhythmias presents various challenges for healthcare professionals, such as adherence to updated diagnostic criteria and understanding of complex arrhythmia mechanisms. Purpose: In this study, we aim to design, implement, and evaluate a guideline-based decision support systems for etiological diagnosis of sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (SMVT), which could potentially address critical challenges associated with the disease diagnosis and management. Methods: To comprehensively capture the semantics embedded in clinical guidelines, we first developed a dedicated knowledge graph tailored to the clinical decision-making. This involved extracting entities and relationships pertinent to key decision procedures from ESC guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias, clinical textbooks or literatures. Subsequently, we translated instances within the knowledge graph into archetypes within openEHR, amplifying the interoperability of clinical information. To enhance the interpretability of the DSS, we established executable diagnostic and treatment processes to offer visual representation of clinical steps in diagnosis and treatment. Ultimately, we constructed a decision support engine to implement the GL-DSS, and its effectiveness was evaluated with anonymous real-world data. Results: The proposed GL-DSS was found to be quite feasible and could provide etiological diagnosis for SMVT. The knowledge base for the constructed GL-DDS included more than 2000 entities and relations, which played a vital role in representing disease pathogenesis. The proposed system can map the clinical entities to a set of openEHR archetypes, thus mitigate the interoperability issues of the hospital information systems and CDSS data integration. Also, this module improved system usability and ensured that guidelines could be easily translated and updated into decision support tools. Real-word medical records from 20 patient were collected for model evaluation, the results showed that the GL-DSS covered most of the entities and relations between diseases and diagnostic evidence recorded in clinical texts and achieved a diagnosis accuracy of 80%. Conclusions: The results demonstrated that our proposed GL-DSS could completely and accurately capture the diagnostic information under the concrete EHR data. Thus, the implement decision support system could have the potential to improve clinical decision-making, patient care, and outcomes in this specialized medical domain. (Figure Presented).

Author: D'Amico, S.; Sauta, E.; Asti, G.; Delleani, M.; Zazzetti, E.; Campagna, A.; Lanino, L.; Maggioni, G.; Ubezio, M.; Todisco, G.; Russo, A.; Tentori, C.A.; Buizza, A.; Franchi, M.; Dall'Olio, L.; Bicchieri, M.; Zampini, M.; Brindisi, M.; Ficara, F.; Riva, E.; Ventura, D.; Crisafulli, L.; Pinocchio, N.; Della Porta, A.; Jacobs, F.; Zambelli, A.; Savevski, V.; Santoro, A.; Sole, F.; Platzbecker, U.; Fenaux, P.; Diez-Campelo, M.; Garcia-Manero, G.; Haferlach, T.; Kordasti, S.; Castellani, G.; Efficace, F.; Santini, V.; Zeidan, A.M.; Komrokji, R.S.; Della Porta, M.G.
Title: A Comprehensive, Artificial Intelligence, Digital Twin Platform Based on Multimodal Real-World Data Integration for Personalized Medicine in Hematology
Abstract Note: Background. Personalized medicine in hematology requires extensive real-world and comprehensive data, including clinical and genomic information. However, integrating, processing and managing such complex data layers in large populations presents significant challenges. Development of patient-tailored models by Artificial Intelligence (AI), known as Digital Twins (DT) offers a novel approach to precision medicine. DT are virtual representations of patients created from multimodal information that can be used to improve diagnosis, prognosis and treatment outcome, improving clinical decision-making. This project aims to advance research by using AI to develop a DT platform for personalized medicine in hematology, with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) as case study. MDS are hematological diseases with high clinical and genomic heterogeneity, presenting a challenging scenario for new technologies implementation Methods. We exploited the Federated Learning platform and technology for Synthetic Data generation developed by the GenoMed4All and Synthema consortia to collect multimodal data from a broad population of MDS patients, in a privacy-complaint manner avoiding data sharing. The multimodal longitudinal data included both structured and unstructured information, encompassing clinical records, genomics, image data, treatments, longitudinal outcomes, and patients reported outcomes. We analyzed 22,080 MDS patients by gathering data using different technological strategies from retrospective cohorts of the international consortium for MDS, prospective Italian MDS registry (FISIM), GIMEMA clinical network, Humanitas Hospital DataLake and Electronic Health Records form the central repository of Lombardia region, Italy Clinical, genomic, and imaging data were organized and integrated into a comprehensive DataLake architecture in common data model format. A Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system with a pre-trained Large Language Model (LLM) was implemented to search, extract and summarize patient information across multiple unstructured text documents and medical records. An innovative AI-based tool was used to capture information on Patient-Reported Outcomes. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) approach was utilized to explain features importance and impact on model prediction. Several AI models were integrated into an interactive and comprehensive DT platform to address relevant clinical questions in MDS patients Results. The DT platform (GEMINI) enables manual entry of individual patient information, including age, sex, blood parameters, gene mutations, cytogenetic abnormalities, morphological and histological features along with clinical questions to address (diagnosis, prognostic assessment, and treatment strategy). First, the DT model infers the conditional dependencies among mutations and classifies individual patients into specific clusters, capturing broad dependencies among genomic alterations. Then, using an AI framework for multimodal analysis in cancer (based on PMID35944502), the DT platform provides personalized estimates of 1) probability of survival, 2) leukemic evolution risk, and 3) response to specific treatments. Using individual clinical and genomic features within a multi-state Markov model, the DT serves as a decision support system to define the optimal timing for therapeutic interventions, focusing on transplantation. Finally, for each disease state and clinical scenario, the DT can simulate changes in quality of life and patient-reported outcomes. This platform, intended for research purposes only, is publicly available (https://gemini-xkb3corsxq-ew.a.run.app/) to help clinicians become familiar with the DT concept. An interactive interface allows users to explore a high-fidelity simulation of the disease's natural history, the impact and timing of therapeutic interventions based on individual patient characteristics Conclusion. GEMINI offers a robust system that supports clinical decision-making, providing a comprehensive overview of the natural history of the disease and the patient's perspective. Our solution benefits from the integration of multiple sources of information in a privacy-compliant manner, avoiding data sharing. DT are expected to improve and accelerate personalized medicine approaches across different hematological diseases with unmet clinical needs

Author: Yung, K.K.Y.; Wu, P.P.Y.; aus der Fünten, K.; Hecksteden, A.; Meyer, T.
Title: Using a Bayesian network to classify time to return to sport based on football injury epidemiological data
Abstract Note: Objective The return-to-sport (RTS) process is multifaceted and complex, as multiple variables may interact and influence the time to RTS. These variables include intrinsic factors of the player, such as anthropometrics and playing position, or extrinsic factors, such as competitive pressure. Providing an individualised estimation is often challenging, and yet clinical decision support tools are often rare in the industry. This study aims to demonstrate the functions of a Bayesian network by the use of a set of basic epidemiological data. Methods To exemplify the use of Bayesian network in sports medicine, such as providing an individualised estimation time to RTS for individual players, we applied Bayesian network to a set of basic epidemiological data. Bayesian network was used as a decision support tool to model the epidemiological data and to integrate clinical data, non-clinical factors and expert knowledge. Specifically, we used the Bayesian network to capture the interaction between variables in order to 1) classify days to RTS and 2) injury severity (minimal, mild, moderate and severe). Results Retrospective injury data of 3374 player seasons and 6143 time-loss injuries from seven seasons of the professional German football league (Bundesliga, 2014/2015 through 2020/2021) were collected from public databases and media resources. A total of twelve variables from three main categories (player’s characteristics and anthropometrics, match information and injury information) were included. The key response variables are 1) days to RTS (1-3, 4-7, 8-14, 15-28, 29-60, >60, and 2) severity (minimal, mild, moderate and severe). As there are more than two categories, producer’s and user’s accuracy was used to reflect the sensitivity and specificity of the model. The producer’s accuracy of the model for days to RTS ranges from 0.24 to 0.97, while for severity categories range from 0.73 to 1.00. The user’s accuracy of the model for days to RTS ranges from 0.52 to 0.83, while for severity categories, it ranges from 0.67 to 1.00. Conclusions The Bayesian network can help to capture different types of data to model the probability of an outcome, such as days to return to sports. In our study, the result from the BN may support coaches and players in predicting days to RTS given an injury, 2) support team planning via assessment of scenarios based on player’s characteristics and injury risk and 3) provide evidence-based support of understanding relationships between factors and RTS. This study shows the key functions and applications of the Bayesian network in RTS, and we suggest further experimenting and developing the Bayesian network into a decision-supporting aid.

Author: Surodina, S.; Volkova, D.; Abdul-Rahman, A.; Borgo, R.
Title: Navigating the Nebula: A Methodology for Expert-Focused Design Study in Complex, Highly Regulated and Stakeholder-Rich Domains. The Case of Ai-Empowered Clinical Data Systems
Abstract Note: Despite the proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, their practical uptake in clinical settings has been lacking progress due to complexities of sociotechnical factors and intricacies of decision-making. Fairness and bias of predictive models, ethics and quality of training data, and corresponding compliance requirements become especially pressing while remaining fuzzy and implicit for various stakeholders who make the decisions. We present learnings and future directions from a methodology for design study with domain experts and propose a novel approach to encoding and collaborative reasoning on complex requirements on the example of AI-Empowered Clinical Decision Support System (AI-CDSS) using a Knowledge Graph (KG) representation. The methodology insights will be useful to the community of visualization researchers and practitioners working across domains for structured requirement and context elicitation and design choices in new, complex, and stakeholder-rich project environments.

Author: Carrilero-Mardones, M.; Delgado-Laguna, A.; Pérez-Martín, J.; Díez, F.J.
Title: Interpretable Models for Bi-Rads Malignancy Classification on Ultrasound
Abstract Note: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, so early and accurate diagnosis is essential. Ultrasound is widely used for detection because it is non-invasive, painless and cost-effective. To standardise the interpretation of ultrasound images, the Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) provides a set of descriptors. However, despite these guidelines, there is only moderate agreement among radiologists, leading to inconsistencies in diagnosis. We collected ultrasound images of 749 breast tumours from three public datasets. Three radiologists assigned them the descriptors and the classification according to the 5th edition of BI-RADS, with a mean intercorrelation of 0.53. Using the descriptors as input, we compared the accuracy and interpretability of several classifiers (multinomial logistic regression, random forests, support vector machines, neural networks, and Bayesian networks) for estimating tumour malignancy. Although there was no significant difference between the models in the qualitative analysis, the Bayesian network performed slightly better, with 0.731 accuracy and 0.674 Cohen's kappa, outperforming other models and providing the most transparent explanations of the diagnostic process. The Bayesian model's ability to reflect the relationships between BI-RADS descriptors and malignancy estimates positions it as a valuable tool for improving diagnostic consistency and enhancing clinical decision support systems. Our work highlights the potential for interpretable models to serve as a support system for non-radiologists and a training tool for novice radiologists.

Author: Bajracharya, R.; Saoulidis, A.; Owusu, O.A.; Acharya, X.; Lo, C.; Jeong, J.; Bajracharya, A.
Title: GUIDELINE-ADHERENT NEURO-SYMBOLIC AI for EXPLAINABLE and PRECISE CLINICAL DECISION SUPPORT in PHARMACOGENOMICS
Abstract Note: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in health care holds transformative potential but continues to face critical challenges, particularly around adherence to clinical guidelines, contextualization to individual patients, and integration of heterogeneous data sources. These limitations raise concerns about reliability, safety, and explainability'core requirements for clinical deployment. The need for transparent and reproducible AI systems is especially pronounced in fields like pharmacogenomics (PGx) and precision medicine, where treatment decisions must be based on well-structured, evidence-based clinical guidelines. To address these issues, the authors present a novel architecture called the Knowledge Augmented Graph Reasoner (KAGR). KAGR is a neuro-symbolic AI framework that enhances Large Language Models (LLMs) by integrating biomedical knowledge graphs with guideline-based reasoning systems. This hybrid approach significantly reduces common problems in generative AI, such as hallucinations and lack of explainability, by embedding structured, guideline-adherent knowledge directly into the reasoning process. KAGR enables LLMs to more reliably interpret and act upon unstructured clinical data by referencing an organized and executable knowledge base. This system supports both reasoning and non-reasoning models in producing clinically accurate outputs that align with validated treatment protocols. In this presentation, we describe the design and evaluation of a KAGR implementation in PGx to build a LLM based guideline adherent decision support tool to provide precision guided treatment optimization recommendation based on PGx guidelines and evidence base. The system demonstrate a high degree of clinical-level accuracy (> 95%) compared to other mainstream baseline approaches to the problem.

Author: Srivastava, T.; Irfan, H.; Swami, S.
Title: From Scarcity to Strategy: Generative AI for Rare Disease Model Conceptualization
Abstract Note: Objectives: Health economic models (HEM) development in rare diseases is often challenging due to multiple factors such as limited patient populations, heterogeneous clinical manifestations, and scarce data on disease progression and outcomes. These issues can complicate model conceptualization and lead to high uncertainty in cost-effectiveness analyses. This proof-of-concept study demonstrates how a proprietary generative AI (Gen-AI) tool—augmented with human feedback, guidelines and domain-specific knowledge—can address these challenges by conceptualizing a HEM for a rare disease with significant data gaps. Methods: A proof-of-concept exercise was undertaken to develop a HEM for Transthyretin amyloid polyneuropathy (ATTR-PN), a rare disease characterized by the accumulation of amyloid protein in nerve tissues. The foundational large language model (LLM) was augmented with several core HEM guidelines to train it, which were chunked, embedded and retrieved via retrieval augmented generation (RAG). To incorporate further contextual awareness, the relationships between training documents were transformed into a knowledge graph via Graph RAG, where nodes represented critical case information and edges depicted relationships among these data points. Hypothetical Document Embedding (HyDE) was employed to enrich embeddings and enhance the AI-driven generation of model concepts. Results: The LLM’s initial recommendation for natural history was further refined using the human-in-loop approach. Initial recommendation was promising and closely aligned with what human experts might have generated through comprehensive manual conceptualization. For the model structure, LLM suggested a semi-Markov model suitable for capturing the complex, non-linear progression of ATTR-PN. It suggested the following health states: Asymptomatic Carrier, Mild Polyneuropathy (PND I), Moderate Polyneuropathy (PND II), Severe Polyneuropathy (PND IIIA and IIIB), End-Stage Polyneuropathy (PND IV). Conclusions: This proof-of-concept exercise illustrates the potential of LLMs to expedite and enhance HEM conceptualization in rare diseases, despite challenges with the inherent data limitations and diverse clinical pathways. Incorporating human feedback is crucial to ensure clinical relevance and methodological rigor.

Author: Yang, Y.; Gao, B.; Tan, C.; Zhu, C.; Yuan, P.; Xie, P.; Gu, Y.; Liu, H.
Title: Ctkgr: Temporal Knowledge Graph Enhanced Prediction of In-Hospital Events for Pneumonia Patients Using Electronic Health Records
Abstract Note: Objective: This study aims to develop an advanced clinical event prediction model leveraging the temporal characteristics embedded within electronic health record (EHR), with a specific focus on predicting clinical events during the hospitalization of pneumonia patients to enhance clinical decision-making.Methods: We constructed a temporal knowledge graph (TKG) by systematically extracting clinical information from pneumonia patient EHR data across multiple time points. To effectively capture temporal dynamics and complex clinical interactions, we introduced the clinical TKG representation (CTKGR) model. This innovative model integrates graph convolutional networks (GCN), recurrent neural networks (RNN), and attention mechanisms to explicitly model clinical event progression. Additionally, a time length-aware module (TLAM) was developed to address challenges posed by irregular time intervals and varying frequencies of patient visits.Results: The proposed CTKGR model exhibited superior predictive performance, achieving an AUC of 0.744 for symptom prediction and 0.797 for medication recommendation tasks, significantly outperforming traditional static and non-temporal methods.Conclusion: The CTKGR model effectively captures the temporal dynamics inherent in clinical data, demonstrating robust predictive capabilities for dynamically evolving clinical events. This study offers a novel and effective framework for AI-driven clinical decision support, with strong potential for application in pneumonia management as well as other clinical domains.

Author: Melendez-Corres, G.; Wahi-Anwar, M.W.; Hoffman, J.M.; Genender, J.; Brown, M.S.
Title: A Multi-Agent Approach for Fully Automated Nephrometry Feature Extraction in CT
Abstract Note: Purpose: Renal lesions are evaluated using scoring systems based on visual assessments and manual measurements. The purpose of this work is to develop a multi-agent system for automated anatomic landmark and nephrometry feature extraction on CT. Methods: Data from a public dataset, containing 489 CT images, corresponding masks for the kidneys and lesions, and clinical data, was split into 70/30 training and test sets. A Cognitive AI framework, SimpleMind, was used to build a multi-agent system. This approach allows the aggregation of segmentation agents and a layer that can reason with their outputs. This reasoning is achieved with agents for feature extraction, spatial inferencing, and fuzzy logic. Agents are configured using a knowledge graph (KG), where each node represents an agent and its parameters, and links represent results being passed between agents. For each image-mask pair, kidney and lesion candidates are post-processed and checked for anatomic consistency. From the kidney masks, relevant anatomic landmarks for nephrometry, such as the urinary collecting system, are derived by spatial inferencing agents. Feature extraction agents take lesion and landmark masks as inputs and compute features used in nephrometry scoring, including lesion diameter, endophycity, distances, overlapping surfaces, etc. To evaluate the utility of the extracted features to predict lesion malignancy and necrosis, Logistic Regression (LR) classifiers were trained and tested against clinical data. Results: The SimpleMind KG successfully extracted landmarks and features across all scans. For malignancy prediction, LR yielded a mean AUC of 0.53±0.10 and 0.61±0.07 on the validation and test sets respectively. For necrosis prediction, LR yielded a mean AUC of 0.89±0.11 and 0.80±0.01 respectively. Conclusion: We developed a multi-agent system that can aggregate segmentation agents and reason with their outputs to automate visual nephrometry scoring. It makes these assessments more feasible in clinical practice and provides explainable decision support using interpretable features.

Author: Kane, M.; Flowers, C.
Title: IBCL-1120: Leveraging Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Knowledge Graphs to Enhance Lymphoma Clinical Research and Decision Support
Abstract Note: The rapid growth of biomedical literature, genomic data, clinical trial findings, and observational data sets have created significant challenges in hematologic oncology and lymphoma research, making it increasingly difficult for researchers to synthesize relevant findings and generate meaningful hypotheses. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into clinical research workflows provides new opportunities to generate scientifically nuanced and rigorous hypotheses and to improve decision-making by leveraging knowledge from the literature. Approach: To address these challenges, we are developing a Lymphoma Retrieval-Augmented Assistant (LYRA), an AI-powered platform designed to support translational research and protocol development in lymphoma. This software system combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with domain-specific knowledge graphs to support research planning and decision-making. The system features a pipeline that ingests scientific publications, clinical guidelines, genomic databases, real-world registries, and institutional clinical trial protocols; extracts named entities; generates vector embeddings; and incorporates them into a structured knowledge base. This enables several key functions: quantifying novelty in the literature using document-similarity metrics, characterizing author expertise with respect to specific diseases and therapeutic areas, and identifying therapeutic trends through temporal analysis of entity co-occurrence. These capabilities support hypothesis generation, team formation, and strategic study design. Named-entity recognition and vector-based semantic search provide the foundation for surfacing contextually relevant findings, while generative models produce tailored outputs for specific research questions. Structured variables—such as disease subtype, biomarkers, end points, and trial phase—are extracted for use in predictive modeling. Validation layers ensure factual consistency and clinical relevance. Conclusion: By integrating AI-driven retrieval and generation with structured biomedical knowledge, this framework supports more efficient, reproducible, and insight-driven engagement with the literature in early-phase oncology research. This work displays the potential of domain-specific RAG systems to transform clinical and translational research in hematologic oncology. By combining intelligent retrieval, language generation, and structured biomedical knowledge, researchers and clinicians can receive timely, accurate, and contextually relevant insights serving as a valuable tool in navigating the complexities of lymphoma research.

Author: Krishnan, P.; Samuel, M.; Canakoglu, A.; Lee, E.; Wu, C.P.; Bhattacharyya, A.; Wong, K.
Title: Precision hemodynamics: Digital twin-guided fluid and vasopressor strategies in shock
Abstract Note: Introduction: Shock is a life-threatening syndrome characterized by inadequate tissue perfusion, necessitating precise hemodynamic monitoring and patient-specific therapeutic adjustments to prevent irreversible organ damage and mortality. Considerable heterogeneity remains in fluid resuscitation and vasopressor titration practices across ICUs. Current fixed treatment algorithms fail to adequately address the dynamic alterations in cardiac output, vascular resistance, and micro-circulation observed in shock progression. This mismatch highlights the critical need for responsive, physiology-driven treatment strategies capable of rapidly adapting to evolving clinical states and preventing multiorgan failure. Objectives: To develop and evaluate a predictive and prescriptive digital twin utilizing deep learning and reinforcement learning to optimize personalized fluid and vasopressor therapy in shock management. Methods: This study utilized electronic medical record (EMR) data' including demographics, comorbidities, hourly vitals, and laboratory values'to build a digital twin-based decision support system. Patients were categorized into five clinical states: hypotension without shock (SCAI A/B), shock (SCAI C/D), refractory shock (SCAI E), discharge, and death. A long-short-term memory (LSTM) model was developed for real-time prediction of shock state transitions within a 2-h prediction window. A directed acyclic graph (DAG) modeled causal relationships between fluid and vasopressor interventions and shock progression. A Q-learning reinforcement learning model was employed to optimize fluid and vasopressor strategies for each clinical state, with interventions adaptively adjusted based on patient responses. An interactive simulator was created, enabling visualization and manipulation of interventions and observing consequent Q value changes. Results: In this retrospective study, data from 2061 ICU patients admitted to Amsterdam University Medical Center were analyzed; patients with EMR data under 24 h were excluded. The digital twin LSTM model showed strong predictive performance, with AUROC values highest for refractory shock (Stage E, AUROC = 0.96) and lower for Stages A (0.85), B (0.81), C (0.82), and D (0.75). Q-learning analysis highlighted that optimal interventions varied according to shock severity and patient subgroup. In general shock states, neutral fluid balance combined with low-dose vasopressors consistently provided optimal outcomes across most cohorts. In refractory shock (extremis shock), cohort-specific strategies emerged; neutral fluid balance with low-dose vasopressors was optimal for cardiac and cardiothoracic surgery patients, while negative fluid balance combined with high-dose vasopressors proved most effective in surgical patients. Conclusions: This study establishes the feasibility and potential clinical value of a digital twin system integrating deep and reinforcement learning for real-time shock trajectory prediction and optimization of fluid and vasopressor management. Future studies will validate this approach across broader patient cohorts and explore advanced reinforcement learning techniques to enhance personalized ICU care.

Author: Zhang, M.; Li, X.
Title: Cost-effectiveness of antiviral treatment for chronic hepatitis B virus infection in China under a standard clinical pathway
Abstract Note: Background: The hepatitis B virus (HBV) epidemic presents a significant global public health challenge, particularly in China. Serious liver diseases such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma caused by the progression of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) are a major contributor of disease burden. High-barrier-to-resistance nucleos (t)ide analogues (NAs) have demonstrated significant efficacy in suppressing HBV DNA replication and delaying HBV-associated complications and the Chinese Medical Association recommends entecavir (ETV), tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF), and tenofovir amibufenamide (TMF) as the first-line therapeutics for CHB patients. This study examined the cost-effectiveness of the four first-line NAs drugs from the perspective of Chinese society, aiming to optimize the allocation of health resources and provide a decision-making basis for international CHB treatment. Method: Based on CHB serological characteristics, patients were stratified into HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative cohorts. An innovative Markov model was developed using Microsoft Excel, incorporating annual cycles over a 60-year simulation period. The treatment protocol was primarily derived from the Chinese Medical Association (CMA) guidelines, model parameters were extracted from published literature and preliminary research. The economic evaluation employed incremental cost-effectiveness ratios benchmarked against predetermined willingness-to-pay thresholds (1 × GDP per capita). Sensitivity analyses were conducted to verify the model robustness. Result: Results showed that TDF (ICER = ¥40,299.17/QALY) and TMF (ICER = ¥40,603.18/QALY) were the most cost-effectiveness options for HBeAg + CHB patients, while TMF (ICER = ¥95,408.08/QALY) were the most cost-effectiveness option for HBeAg- CHB. One-way sensitivity analyses identified the most influential parameters: the transfer probability from HBeAg + CHB to HBsAg serological clearance and the transfer probability from HBeAg- CHB to complete virological response. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis indicated 100% probability of cost-effectiveness for all four treatments (ETV, TDF, TAF, and TMF) in HBeAg + CHB, whereas none achieved cost-effectiveness in HBeAg- CHB patients. Scenario analyses from a healthcare system perspective demonstrated TMF as the sole cost-effective option for HBeAg- CHB patients. In scenarios incorporating generic medications, TAF and TDF emerged as the most cost-effective options for HBeAg-positive and HBeAgnegative CHB patients, respectively. The results remained robust across variations in treatment duration (30 or 40 years). Conclusion: For HBeAg + CHB patients, TDF/TMF → ETV is more cost-effective, whereas for HBeAg-CHB patients, TMF → ETV is more likely to be cost-effective than other treatment regimens, despite exceeding WTP.

Author: Noben, Ö.; Kılıç, Ö.D.; Rienstra, T.; Dumontier, M.; Celebi, R.
Title: Rule-Augmented Constraint Learning for Semantic Error Detection in MIMIC-III Knowledge Graph
Abstract Note: High-quality, error-free data is essential for developing reliable data-driven models, particularly in clinical decision support systems where inaccurate predictions can have serious consequences. While Knowledge Graphs (KGs) offer a structured and semantically rich representation for clinical data, ensuring their consistency and correctness remains a challenge. Existing rule mining techniques provide solutions to the automatic extraction of logical constraints from KGs, but they often produce redundant or clinically irrelevant rules, especially when dealing with numeric or categorical literals such as age or lab values. KG constraints - rules intended to capture implausible or conflicting facts in the KG, can be used to spot semantic errors: facts that might conform to the underlying schema but contradict with domain knowledge. In this work, we propose a novel framework for constraint learning in clinical KGs that identifies and transforms high-confidence rules into clinically plausible constraints. We propose two approaches, based on class disjointness and literal clustering combined with rule mining. We validate the clinical relevance of these generated rules using expert-curated constraints and large language models (LLMs). The results on the MIMIC-III clinical dataset show that rule filtering based constraint learning effectively preserves clinically meaningful rules that align with established medical knowledge. For numeric data, we achieve reliable value groupings through our clustering-based method, and the rules derived from these groupings were validated by Large Language Models (LLMs). Their outputs confirm the clinical relevance of a portion of those discovered rules. By providing interpretable and scalable solutions to semantic inconsistencies in KGs, this study contributes to increasing the KG trustworthiness and its clinical usability.

Author: Song, I.S.; Choi, M.H.; Lee, J.H.; Lee, J.C.; Song, Y.G.
Title: A Hybrid Al Agent for Precision Antibiotic Prescribing
Abstract Note: Background: Empirical antibiotic prescribing is frequently performed outside infectious-disease specialties under constraints such as limited diagnostics, delayed consultation, and regional variation in antimicrobial resistance. Adherence to standardized guidelines remains low, leading to inappropriate therapy. Data-driven clinical decision support framework that integrates patient context with validated guideline may improve prescribing consistency and antimicrobial stewardship. Methods: We developed a hybrid artificial intelligence (Al) agent designed to provide empirical antibiotic recommendation with evidence-based reasoning through an integrated pipeline. In the first stage, a machine-learning (ML) module predicts infection-related outcomes, including culture positivity, likely pathogens, mortality risk, and the most appropriate empirical antibiotic class, based on patient vital signs and laboratory data. This ML-based recommendation serves as the initial prescribing suggestion. In the second stage, the agent refines and validates this suggestion through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reasoning across three complementary knowledge modalities: (1) guideline-guided RAG, retrieving curated Sanford Guide and K-APP content from a VectorDB to ensure alignment with institutional and international standards; (2) graph-guided RAG, leveraging a structured knowledge graph that encodes relationships among syndromes, pathogens, and antibiotics to provide explainable, rule-consistent reasoning: and (3) web-search-guided RAG, dynamically retrieving the most up-to-date medical literature and consensus statements from verified sources. For evaluation, anonymized antibiotic prescriptions from two general hospitals in South Korea (2006-2023; 950,000 cases) were analyzed, with 10,000 cases randomly selected for retrospective comparison. A clinician-prompted LLM-as-Judge powered by an open-source 120B-parameter reasoning model (oss-120B) securely hosted on our internal GPU servers, evaluated Al-generated recommendations against historical physician prescriptions using a Hybrid Score integrating clinical assessment and semantic similarity to consultation notes. Results: Among 9,899 evaluated cases, the ML module achieved AUROC with its 95% confidence interval (95% CI) = 0.805 (culture positivity), 0.853 (pathogen ID), 0.921 (antibiotic recommendation), and 0.886 (mortality). The web-search RAG achieved the highest hybrid score (37.0% win rate), outperforming the knowledge-graph RAG (32.7%) and guideline RAG (30.1%). Web-search RAG excelled in dosing accuracy, evidence quality, and resistance awareness, while knowledge-graph RAG achieved higher safety and clinical appropriateness through structured reasoning. Semantic similarity with consultation notes averaged 0.22, with the web-search RAG highest in contextual match. Conclusions: This retrospectively validated, multi-source framework integrates ML-based empirical prescribing, three RAG modalities, and consultation-note-grounded LLM-as-Judge evaluation. By leveraging 950,000 real prescriptions and 10,000 patient datasets. it demonstrates scalable, explainable antibiotic decision support. The framework is being scaled to 500,000 cases and validated externally using the independently preprocessed and standardized MIMIC-IV dataset Hospital-level deployment ongoing for prospective trials on prescribing efficiency and the reduction of antimicrobial misuse reduction. Ultimately, may serve as reliable decision support to system for healthcare institutions lacking in-house specialists, thereby promoting appropriate antibiotic use and advancing global antimicrobial stewardship through transparent, data-driven AI reasoning.

Author: Sesen, M.B.; Yeung, J.A.; Asgari, E.
Title: Development and validation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and GraphRAG for complex clinical cases
Abstract Note: Objective Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is a progressive condition requiring evidence-based management, but adherence to complex guidelines remains challenging. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support clinical decision-making, yet their unreliability limits direct use. This study aimed to evaluate whether Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), particularly a knowledge graph-enhanced pipeline (GraphRAG), improves guideline-based clinical decision support (CDS) in CKD management. Methods and Analysis We compared three approaches: a baseline LLM (GPT-4o), a vector-indexed RAG pipeline, and a GraphRAG pipeline. Each model answered nine clinically relevant questions for a synthetic cohort of 70 CKD patients. Outputs were assessed for clinical correctness, patient-specificity, and clarity, using both clinician-led evaluations and an LLM-as-Judge framework. Results RAG-based methods outperformed the baseline LLM in clinical correctness and guideline adherence. GraphRAG achieved the highest patient-specificity by leveraging multi-hop relationships across a knowledge graph derived from NICE CKD guidelines, particularly for tasks involving thresholds, algorithmic decisions, or open-ended management. However, GraphRAG scored lower in clarity, as its graph walks often returned long guideline excerpts that obscured key recommendations. All RAG systems were limited by the scope of the indexed guideline and performed poorly when essential information was missing. Conclusions RAG and GraphRAG provide a scalable, auditable foundation for guideline-aligned CDS in CKD, with GraphRAG showing particular strengths in tailoring advice to patient data. Nonetheless, trade-offs remain between specificity and clarity, and effective deployment will require robust content management, transparent validation pipelines, and integration within established clinical governance frameworks.

Author: Chen, S.; Yang, Y.
Title: Implementation of Large Language Model and GraphRAG-Assisted Decision Support for Multidisciplinary Team Cancer Care
Abstract Note: Introduction: Lung cancer remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with late diagnosis and misdiagnosis signifi cantly impacting survival rates. Current multidisciplinary team (MDT) workflows are hindered by data fragmentation, inconsistent inter pretation of guidelines, and limited integration of trial results. While traditional AI-powered Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) have improved diagnostic accuracy and personalized treatment options, they still face limitations in data retrieval, contextual reasoning, and decision traceability. To address these challenges, we evaluated a novel approach combining large language models (LLMs) with GraphRAG technology. Methods: We selected DeepSeek-R1, a reinforcement learning enhanced large language model, as foundation model for contextual reasoning and treatment option matching. We then devel oped a comprehensive knowledge graph integrating patient data from multiple sources, where nodes represented clinical entities (e.g., gene mutations, treatment types) and edges defined relationships between them. Publicly available clinical guidelines and evidences (e.g., NCCN, CSCO, industry consensus, abstracts from WCLC) were incorporated as reference nodes linked to patient-specific nodes to provide management recommendations. We retrospectively analyzed 283 MDT cases from January 2021 to February 2025 for model training and prospectively validated the performance of this approach in 8 real-world MDT cases through an Investigator-Initiated Trial (IIT). The LLM and GraphRAG-assisted recommendations were compared against MDT expert consensus decisions in our hospital. The primary outcome was agreement rate with MDT expert consensus. Exploratory outcomes included time to diagnosis and accuracy of decision traceability. Results: The LLM and GraphRAG-assisted approach achieved an alignment rate of 88.9% (16/18) with MDT expert consensus. Misalignment occurred due to failure in clinical entity extraction for a patient undergoing multiple treatment lines and uncollected innovative clinical findings (e.g., LAURA trial data) during graph construction. For exploratory endpoints, the average response genera tion time was 3.2 minutes, significantly faster than the traditional expertconsensus mode (5.6 minutes). The model demonstrated 100% traceability for recommended treatment options, including their sources and source links. Conclusions: The LLM and GraphRAG-assisted approach represents an innovative AI tool that enhances the accuracy and effi ciency of lung cancer MDT discussions. Future development should focus on prospective validation across diverse patient populations and inte gration with existing clinical systems to maximize adoption and improve patient outcomes.

Author: Alqahtani, Y.M.; Alhameed, M.H.; Zogan, H.; Amin, S.T.; Metwally, A.A.; Abdalraheem, M.H.O.
Title: Deep Learning Frameworks for Drug Discovery and Clinical Decision Support
Publication Title: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
Abstract Note: Deep learning has emerged as a game changer in the medical sector, and has played a significant role in drug discovery and clinical decision support systems. The paper presents a multimodal, feedback-based system that unites these regions into one complex deep learning system. The framework uses a variety of biomedical data streams, such as molecular folds, genome sequences, electronic health records, and medical imaging, to empower a holistic analysis and decision-making. Convolutional neural networks, graph neural networks, transformer models and reinforcement learning are advanced models that are used to solve important problems in drug discovery, like target identification and molecular optimization, and clinical problems like diagnosis, prognosis and treatment recommendation. Experimental analysis in the form of a case study shows that the integrated framework outperforms the standalone techniques, especially in multimodal situations. The adaptability and predictive power of the model are also associated with the mechanism of feedback that includes the clinical outcomes. The problems of the data privacy, interpretability, and scalability are discussed, and the potential solutions to them can be explained in the context of the artificial intelligence explainable and federated learning. The proposed framework is a viable and adaptable approach to the transition to precision medicine and smart healthcare.

Title: Clinical Study on an Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Chest Radiograph Model Based on Big Data and Deep Learning for Early Detection of Kawasaki Disease
Abstract Note: Brief Summary The goal of this observational study is to develop an AI-based early warning system for Kawasaki Disease (KD) using chest X-rays (CXR) in children diagnosed with Kawasaki Disease. The main question\[s\] it aims to answer are: 1. Can AI modeling of CXR features help identify high-risk KD patients earlier than current diagnostic methods? 2. Can the AI system predict the optimal IVIG treatment window and coronary artery risks in KD patients? Participants will: Provide retrospective data on chest X-rays and clinical data (CRP, coronary ultrasound, etc.) Allow analysis of CXR features using deep learning models to extract relevant patterns Have their data incorporated into a federated learning model to ensure privacy and data security Detailed Description 1. Research Background and Clinical Pain Points Kawasaki Disease (KD) is a leading cause of acquired heart disease in children. Traditional diagnosis relies on subjective symptoms such as fever lasting ≥5 days and rashes, leading to two major problems: delayed diagnosis, with 30% of atypical patients missing the optimal IVIG treatment window (fever duration of 5-10 days); and coronary artery damage: delaying treatment for ≥7 days increases the risk of coronary dilation by 47%. The current AHA standards have only a 35% sensitivity for children with fever ≤3 days, highlighting the urgent need to establish an objective early warning system. 2. Research Objectives and Technical Approach Core breakthrough: First time using routine chest X-rays (CXR) to develop an AI-based early warning model. Technical path: Multi-center data integration, collection of CXR and clinical data (clinical symptoms, laboratory tests, coronary ultrasound, etc.), and a federated learning framework to ensure privacy and security. Exploration of imaging biomarkers and CXR features that are invisible to the human eye, as well as the development of a multi-modal dynamic early warning model. Dual-path CNN to extract CXR features → Graph neural networks to integrate laboratory indicators → Diagnosis model to output the risk score of kawasaki disease.↑ 3. Innovation Advantages and Clinical Value Early-warning performance was strong by day 3 of fever, achieving a pre-trial sensitivity of 87.2% for Kawasaki disease, while providing individualized IVIG treatment windows and predicted coronary-artery risk. The lightweight model (less than 50MB) is adaptable for use in primary care settings. Clinical pathway: AI identifies high-risk children → Priority for echocardiography → IVIG treatment window advanced → Reduction in cardiovascular complications. The ultimate goal is to shorten diagnosis time and reduce cardiovascular complications of KD patients in China. 4. Validation Plan and Results Translation Three-phase validation: Internal: 5-fold cross-validation (AUC ≥0.88) External: Blind testing in 3 hospitals (sensitivity \>85%, specificity \>80%) Clinical: Real-time deployment in emergency settings (response time ≤15 seconds) Results translation: 1-2 peer-reviewed journal publications and 1-2 patent filings; facilitating early identification of Kawasaki disease, thereby improving clinical outcomes. 5. Key Conclusion This study aims to decode objective biomarkers such as pulmonary artery vascular signs in CXR images and construct the AI-CXR early warning system for KD. It will break through the current reliance on fever duration and subjective symptoms, providing support for early diagnosis and improving patient outcomes.

Author: Anand, V.S.; Akhil, V.V.
Title: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems for Medical Decision Support: A Comprehensive Survey
Abstract Note: The introduction of Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation Technology is a breakthrough in the field of Medical Artificial Intelligence, allowing autonomous agents to coordinate complex clinical workflows, integrate evidence into the patient’s care cycle, and supply decision-making support to health care professionals and patients. In this manuscript, we will offer a comprehensive analysis of the architectures of Agentic RAG technology and its numerous applications and approaches within healthcare. More specifically, we will systematically evaluate the various types of multi-agentic systems that may be employed for specific professional and clinical tasks, such as diagnostic reasoning, medical question answering, report generation, drug discovery, and optimizing overall healthcare delivery. Aspects of the technical architecture that will be addressed in this review are the integration of knowledge graphs to represent knowledge, multi-modal reasoning capabilities, mechanisms to support adherence to clinical guidelines, and creation of interpretable decision-making frameworks. In addition to these key technological developments, the author will also address a variety of challenges encountered when developing agentic RAG systems, including clinical validation, collaboration between health care providers and AI, ethical issues, and deploying agentic RAG technology in health care settings that have limited resources. Lastly, this review provides an overarching conceptual framework for understanding how agentic RAG technology can assist in supporting physicians, nursing staff, health care personnel, and patients with a variety of tasks across multiple disciplines, while also supporting many of the key safety, privacy, and responsible considerations related to AI in health care. This review identifies architecturally based patterns in medical agentic systems.

Author: Kumar, A.; Quante, M.; Bojti, I.; Wehrle, J.; Hornecker, A.; Amft, O.; Cypko, M.A.
Title: KI-COMPASS: causality-aware digital patient models with an example in cardio-oncology
Publication Title: International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery
Abstract Note: Purpose We propose a causality-aware modelling framework for digital patient models with use-case in cardio-oncological care. Oncological treatments may affect cardiovascular health through complex physiological pathways, treatment interactions, and patient-specific risk factors. Clinical experts therefore face trade-offs between effective cancer therapy and cardiovascular safety. Clinical decision-support for such trade-offs require patient-specific assessment of longitudinal effects across treatments, comorbidities, and risk factors. However, model development and validation are challenging because real-world clinical data is inherently heteorgenous, longitudinal, and often irregularly sampled. Relevant information spans across multiple modalities and domains including physiological measurements, medication histories, laboratory results, unstructured clinical text, and wearable-derived signals. Digital patient models aim to provide patient-specific virtual representations using real-world clinical data, and support queries under hypothetical intervention scenarios [1]. However, existing modelling approaches often rely either on data-driven multi-modal models with limited causal interpretability, or use causal models that are difficult to scale to high-dimensional clinical data. Cardio-oncology is inherently multi-disciplinary, therefore, a digital patient model should facilitate structured contributions from clinical and technical experts and support transparent governance of model assumptions aligned with societal requirements including safety, accountability and equitable use. To address these limitations, we present a cooperative framework that unifies multi-modal generative modelling and expert-curated dynamic causal structures for cardio-oncological care scenario. Methods The framework targets the core requirement of digital patient models: simulation of what-if scenarios under alternative treatment and disease progression assumptions. Current modelling strategies fall in two categories: multi-modal representation models and expert-curated knowledge or causal graphs. Multi-modal embedding models can integrate heterogeneous, high-dimensional real-world clinical data, however, mainly support predictive tasks and remain limited to correlations. Conversely, causal models with explicit semantics often face limitations in scalability and data integration. The proposed framework combines representation learning with expert-curated temporal causal structures to support prediction and simulation under hypothetical interventions. Effective causality-aware modeling requires coordinated input from oncology, cardio-oncology, data science, machine learning, and knowledge engineering. Accordingly, the framework defines interaction points for data preparation, causal curation and validation, model training, and clinical simulation, together with documentation of modeling assumptions. Results Figure 1 illustrates the framework. Multi-modal patient observations (Fig. 1: B), comprise longitudinal clinical data and unstructured text. A multi-modal embedding model encodes patient observarions into a latent space (Fig. 1: C) with periodic updates as new data becomes available (Fig. 1: b). The latent representation is regularised using an expert-curated Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBN) (Fig. 1: D) to enforce clinically meaningful causal structure. The regularised model (M) is used for’’what-if‘‘simulations (Fig. 1: d). A state transition module (Fig. 1: V) handles temporal evolution i.e., simulation of future latent states (Fig. 1: h) and a control module (Fig. 1: S) i.e., a decision-making function that maps latent state to an intervention (Fig. 1: p). The control module will be based on a guideline-based or an expert-defined policy. The approach is inspired by causalVAE [2] and causal disentanglement, which constrains latent variables to follow a predefined causal structure learnt from data. In prior pre-work on a cohort of kidney transplant recipients, we assessed whether observational data alone can support enforcement of causal structure in latent dimensions. The findings demonstrated that the data-only approaches are insufficient for capturing causal structure in complex healthcare domains and motivate the explicit integration of expert-curated causal structures. In contrast to data-driven causal discovery, our proposed framework uses causal structures derived from expert curation, clinical guidelines, and mechanistic understanding. The DBN represents temporal dependencies between latent factors and provide an interpretable state representation for simulation. What-if scenarios correspond to interventions on selected latent variables that remain consistent with causal structure and support simulation of alternative treatment strategies or patient trajectories. As part of our cooperative(Figure presented)system, oncologists and cardio-oncologists curate and validate the DBN (Fig. 1: c), data scientists prepare and manage observational data, and model scientists optimise representation learning under expert-defined causal constraints. At the point of care, clinicians interact with the digital patient model through a simulation interface (Fig. 1: e) and evaluate alternative oncological therapies or cardioprotective strategies with projected downstream cardiovascular outcomes. Transparent causal structure support clinical interpretation beyond opaque risk estimates. Beyond individual decision support, aggregated scenario-based analyses of care pathways can support evaluation of equitable AI use and may inform guideline updates, health policy planning, and resource allocation. Governance artifacts including documented assumptions, validation results, and intended-use constraints support alignment with requirements for safety, accountability, and equitable use. Conclusion We present a causality-aware modelling framework for digital patient models that combines multi-modal generative modelling with expert-curated dynamic causal structures in cardio-oncology. The framework addresses a limitation of purely correlational multi-modal modelling when the goal is what-if simulation. Incorporation of expert-curated causal structures into the latent representation supports simulations, interpretability, and clinically grounded counterfactual analysis. A cooperative design with explicit roles and governance artifacts supports multidisciplinary adoption and alignment with broader safety and accountability requirements. Causality-aware digital patient models can move beyond predictive modeling toward clinically actionable decision support under explicit causal assumptions.

Author: Yang, L.; Wan, H.; Zhu, J.; Zhou, P.; Wang, Z.
Title: Knowledge-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for Personalized Oncology Treatment Recommendation Based on Multi-Modal Medical Knowledge Graph
Abstract Note: Personalized oncology treatment recommendation is a critical clinical task that requires integrating complex, multi-modal patient data with established medical knowledge to ensure both accuracy and safety. While deep learning models excel at capturing latent patterns from high-dimensional data, their opaque decision-making processes and inability to strictly enforce clinical constraints hinder their adoption in high-stakes medical domains. Conversely, traditional rule-based systems offer high interpretability but struggle to scale with complex, heterogeneous data. To address these challenges, we propose the Knowledge-driven Neuro-Symbolic Network (K-NeSyNet), a novel framework for personalized oncology treatment recommendation. K-NeSyNet is grounded in a newly constructed Multi-Modal Oncology Knowledge Graph (MM-OKG) that unifies genomic mutations, medical imaging features, clinical text, and structured medical guidelines from publicly available sources including TCGA, DGIdb, KEGG, and NCCN guidelines. The core innovation of K-NeSyNet is a three-channel differentiable symbolic reasoning mechanism that explicitly models guideline recommendations, mutation-target matching, and contraindication penalties for each patient-drug pair. These symbolic signals are dynamically fused with the outputs of a knowledge-aware graph attention neural reasoning module via an adaptive gated fusion network. Crucially, the fusion gate learns to balance neural and symbolic confidence in a patient-specific manner, while contraindication evidence enters both the symbolic score and a dedicated safety objective to down-weight clinically risky drugs. Extensive experiments on a real-world multi-modal oncology dataset comprising 4,781 patients across 10 cancer types demonstrate that K-NeSyNet consistently outperforms eight state-of-the-art baselines. Specifically, K-NeSyNet achieves the highest F1@10 of 0.9227, NDCG@10 of 0.9656, and Jaccard similarity of 0.9366, while maintaining competitive Clinical Guideline Consistency. Ablation studies confirm the indispensable role of each component, with the removal of the fusion gate causing the most significant performance degradation. Furthermore, K-NeSyNet provides transparent, score-decomposed explanations for its recommendations, offering a crucial step toward trustworthy AI-assisted clinical decision support.

Author: Ait Bigane, Y.; Ben-Bouazza, F.-E.; Edder, A.; Emssaad, I.; Sangare, D.; Manchadi, O.; Jioudi, B.
Title: A Neuro-Symbolic Clinical Agent for cardiovascular risk stratification: Integrating stacking ensembles with simulation-augmented reasoning
Abstract Note: This research presents a Neuro-Symbolic Clinical Agent for cardiovascular risk assessment that integrates ensemble machine learning with tightly coupled counterfactual simulation and targeted guideline retrieval. The framework is trained and validated on the CAIR-CVD-2025 dataset using a hybrid stacking architecture, where CatBoost, Random Forest, and a specialized neural network implement the neural risk prediction module of the proposed system. The ensemble achieved the highest discriminative performance with an ROC-AUC of 0.872 (95% CI: 0.836–0.910) and demonstrated excellent calibration with a Brier Score of 0.148, consistent with established benefits of ensemble-based risk prediction. Beyond prediction, the system functions as an active reasoning agent that performs simulation-guided inference: a local SHAP layer identifies patient-specific risk drivers, while a rule-based simulation engine executes “what-if” experiments to quantify the risk reduction achievable through specific interventions (e.g., lipid management). To address the “reasoning gap”, the reporting module utilizes a “Safe RAG” protocol, guiding guideline retrieval through SHAP-identified risk drivers to prevent hallucinations. Automated assessment confirmed that the LLaMA-3.3-70B generation layer achieved high faithfulness (0.89) to ESC/AHA guidelines. These findings indicate that predictive accuracy, probabilistic reliability, and evidence-based reasoning can coexist within a transparent, agentic decision-support system.

Author: Pan, Y.; Tang, H.; Wang, Z.; Lev, B.
Title: Guideline-Bound or Case-Adaptive? A Guideline–Case Evidence-Balancing Framework for Clinical LLMs
Abstract Note: Clinical large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate diagnostic and therapeutic recommendations, yet their decision knowledge is often difficult to govern. Clinical guidelines provide normative authority, standardization, and safety boundaries, whereas real-world cases capture contextual adaptation for patients with comorbidities, contraindications, and complex medication histories. This study examines how these knowledge sources can be positioned and fused for clinical decision support without reducing the system to either rigid guideline retrieval or unguided case imitation. We propose GCE-LLM, a Guideline–Case Evidence-Balancing framework for clinical LLMs in heart failure treatment decision support. The framework retains the technical strength of LLM-KG bidirectional augmentation: LLMs structure guideline knowledge into a computable clinical knowledge graph, and the graph together with a case base constrains downstream LLM generation. GCE-LLM builds a dual-source knowledge base from heart failure guidelines and 5,620 real-world patients in the HERO cohort, retrieves guideline and case evidence through hybrid semantic and keyword mechanisms, applies contraindication filtering and source-aware reranking, and generates structured treatment plans through clinically constrained prompting. We evaluated GCE-LLM against six baseline configurations using blind assessments by 50 cardiology experts, producing 2,800 expert-plan evaluations across simple and complex scenarios. GCE-LLM achieved the highest overall performance, with the clearest advantage in complex scenarios. The findings contribute to decision support systems research by showing how clinical LLMs can be designed as evidence-governed, case-adaptive, and auditable decision-support artifacts rather than as unconstrained generators.

Author: Shellum, Jane L.; Nishimura, Rick A.; Milliner, Dawn S.; Harper, Charles M. Jr; Noseworthy, John H.
Title: Knowledge management in the era of digital medicine: A programmatic approach to optimize patient care in an academic medical center.
Abstract Note: INTRODUCTION: The pace of medical discovery is accelerating to the point where caregivers can no longer keep up with the latest diagnosis or treatment  recommendations. At the same time, sophisticated and complex electronic medical  records and clinical systems are generating increasing volumes of patient data,  making it difficult to find the important information required for patient care.  To address these challenges, Mayo Clinic established a knowledge management  program to curate, store, and disseminate clinical knowledge. METHODS: The  authors describe AskMayoExpert, a point-of-care knowledge delivery system, and  discuss the process by which the clinical knowledge is captured, vetted by  clinicians, annotated, and stored in a knowledge content management system. The  content generated for AskMayoExpert is considered to be core clinical content and  serves as the basis for knowledge diffusion to clinicians through order sets and  clinical decision support rules, as well as to patients and consumers through  patient education materials and internet content. The authors evaluate  alternative approaches for better integration of knowledge into the clinical  workflow through development of computer-interpretable care process models.  RESULTS: Each of the modeling approaches evaluated has shown promise. However,  because each of them addresses the problem from a different perspective, there  have been challenges in coming to a common model. Given the current state of  guideline modeling and the need for a near-term solution, Mayo Clinic will likely  focus on breaking down care process models into components and on standardization  of those components, deferring, for now, the orchestration. CONCLUSION: A  point-of-care knowledge resource developed to support an individualized approach  to patient care has grown into a formal knowledge management program. Translation  of the textual knowledge into machine executable knowledge will allow integration  of the knowledge with specific patient data and truly serve as a colleague and  mentor for the physicians taking care of the patient.

Author: Anny Leema, A.; Rajashri, S.; Sriram, Mukundan; Girish, Makam; Balakrishnan, P.
Title: MMCRAG-Resp: a multi-modal corrective retrieval-augmented generation framework for explainable respiratory disease reasoning.
Abstract Note: BACKGROUND: Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems only use semantic similarity to retrieve information, and since this method is quite  limiting, it may find clinically irrelevant evidence and produce outputs that are  unsafe or hallucinated. This drawback is particularly important in respiratory  care, where the diagnosis relies heavily on very accurate physiological  indicators such as spirometry patterns and symptom profiles. METHODS: We propose  MMCRAG-Resp., a clinically grounded, physiology-aware corrective RAG framework  for respiratory intelligence. The system harmonizes 17,516 patient records from  three heterogeneous public datasets (Respiratory Sound Database, NHANES  spirometry, and clinical guidelines) through a unified respiratory ontology.  Multi-modal embeddings (acoustic, spirometric, and textual) are fused into  144-dimensional vectors and indexed in FAISS. A novel Respiratory Relevance Score  (RRS) combining spirometric pattern agreement (weight 0.45), symptom overlap  (0.30), and embedding similarity (0.25) gates evidence quality before LLM  consumption via a three-path correction policy. A locally deployed small language  model (Ollama; llama3.2, Mistral-7B-Instruct) generates evidence-constrained,  fully traceable clinical explanations without GPU requirements. RESULTS:  Evaluated on 200 held-out test queries drawn from the harmonized corpus,  MMCRAG-Resp achieved a Clinical Precision@10 of 0.81, a Hallucination Rate of  0.11 (71% relative reduction over Vanilla RAG), a Spirometry Alignment Score of  0.79, and an Evidence Citation Rate of 0.87. Ablation studies confirmed that  spirometry-first scoring contributes the largest single-component gain. All  pairwise comparisons with baselines were statistically significant (p < 0.001,  McNemar's test; Cohen's d = 1.42). CONCLUSION: MMCRAG-Resp is, to the best of our  knowledge, the first system combining multi-modal respiratory evidence retrieval,  physiologically-grounded corrective RAG, and privacy-preserving local LLM  inference in a single deployable clinical reasoning framework. The approach  advances safe, explainable AI-assisted respiratory decision support.
